newsitem.title: GERMANY: New book unveiled on brave Germans who saved Jews.
newsitem.headline: New book unveiled on brave Germans who saved Jews.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Friday hailed a new book about ordinary Germans who risked their lives in the Nazi era to save Jews from the Holocaust, but admitted these were the exception.

"It is incredible how many simple people -- farmers, people in the circus -- tried to help...But it was a minority who had the courage to resist...Most Germans did not," Kinkel told the launch of the book entitled "Other Germans under Hitler".

Author Herbert Straeten said he was not trying to challenge a recent controversial book by U.S. historian Daniel Goldhagen which argued that most Germans were willing accomplices of Hitler because of what he said was a deep-seated anti-Semitism.
"This was never meant to be an answer to Goldhagen. It has been planned for years," Straeten told guests including Israeli ambassador Avraham Primor and some people featured in his book.
"I don't believe in Goldhagen's thesis, but I still say 'too few, too few'," Straeten said, referring to the fact that few Germans were brave enough to resist the Nazi regime.
"Those were terrible times and we all know what came out of them," said Straeten, 70, who was captured by advancing Russian troops in 1945 as a young soldier in the German army.
Of 12,000 Europeans honoured by Israel as "the just ones among the people" only 300 are German. But Straeten says ten times as many helped Jews indirectly.
The book, subtitled with the Jewish saying: "Every person who saves one life saves the whole world", tells the story of 26 ordinary Germans who saved Jews' lives.
Straeten said Oskar Schindler, a German industrialist who saved 1,200 Jewish workers made famous in the recent film "Schindler's List", was just one of many.

Circus owner, Adolf Althoff, hid a Jewish woman and her two daughters amongst his troupe, which travelled across Nazi-occupied Europe. "Circus people don't ask if you are Christian, Jewish or heathen," Althoff said in the book.
Straeten called lawyer Hans Georg Calmeyer "probably the most sucessful German resistance fighter against Hitler."

Calmeyer, posted to the Netherlands during World War Two in the German army, saved the lives of thousands of Dutch Jews by forging their documents to let them pass as "half-Jews" and thus avoid Nazi concentration camps.
Baroness Celina von Mirbach hid Jewish friends who had once played the piano with her in her society music circle.
Straeten said it was unlikely sales of his book could top Goldhagen's "Hitler's Willing Executioners", which shot to the top of the best-sellers list when it was published in German last year.
He said the new debate into the question of German guilt and responsibility during the Nazi years had been sparked by interest from the younger generation half a century on.
"It's not the sons who are asking the questions now but the grandchildren," Straeten said.

In the epilogue to Straeten's book, the leader of Germany's Jewish community Ignatz Bubis wrote: "The Holocaust will continue to weigh down German-Jewish relations for many years, but we must give the next generation examples of tolerance, humanity and civil courage."
